prompt: Use the limit definition of the derivative to find $f'(2)$ for $f(x) = \frac{1}{x}$. Give your answer as a fraction.
hint: Set up $\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\frac{1}{2 + h} - \frac{1}{2}}{h}$. Combine the two fractions on top first.

hints.text: Set up $\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\frac{1}{2 + h} - \frac{1}{2}}{h}$. Combine the two fractions on top first.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up: $\frac{1}{2 + h} - \frac{1}{2} = \frac{2 - (2 + h)}{2(2 + h)} = \frac{-h}{2(2 + h)}$. Notice an $h$ appeared on top, ready to cancel.
Divide the combined fraction by $h$, which cancels the $h$ on top: $\frac{-h}{2(2 + h) \cdot h} = \frac{-1}{2(2 + h)}$. Now let $h \to 0$.
Letting $h \to 0$ turns the fraction into $\frac{-1}{2 \cdot 2}$, so the derivative is $f'(2) = -\frac{1}{4}$.

explanation: Combine the fractions in the numerator over a common denominator: $f(2 + h) - f(2) = \frac{1}{2 + h} - \frac{1}{2} = \frac{2 - (2 + h)}{2(2 + h)} = \frac{-h}{2(2 + h)}$.
Divide by $h$, which cancels the $h$ on top and leaves $\frac{-1}{2(2 + h)}$.
Let $h \to 0$: $f'(2) = \frac{-1}{4}$. The tangent at $(2, \frac{1}{2})$ slopes gently downward.

alternativeExplanations.title: Sanity check with secants
steps: Compute the secant slope from $x = 2$ to $x = 2.1$: $\frac{1/2.1 - 1/2}{0.1} = \frac{0.47619 - 0.5}{0.1} \approx -0.238$.
Shorten the step to $0.01$: the slope from $2$ to $2.01$ is $\frac{0.497512 - 0.5}{0.01} \approx -0.249$.
The slopes are heading to $-0.25 = -\frac{1}{4}$. A negative slope makes sense because $\frac{1}{x}$ decreases as $x$ grows.

alternativeExplanations.title: Use the power rule
steps: Rewrite the function with a negative exponent, $f(x) = x^{-1}$, so the power rule applies.
Bring the exponent down and lower it by one: $f'(x) = -1 \cdot x^{-2} = -\frac{1}{x^2}$.
At $x = 2$ this gives $-\frac{1}{4}$, the same value the limit definition produces after much more algebra.
